pr_title: Show common commands when calling `rails -h` outside a Rails dir
pr_body:
### Motivation

When running `rails -h` or just `rails` outside a Rails application, Rails outputs all options for running the `rails new` command. This can be confusing to users when they probably want to see the common Rails commands.

Instead, we should always show the common commands when running `rails -h` inside or outside a Rails application.

### Detail

With this change help works as follows...

Outside a Rails application we never show the extended commands: db:migrate, etc...
The extended commands require a Rails application. They also take up a lot screen space.

- `rails`        outputs the help for the gem commands
- `rails -h`     outputs the help for the gem commands.
- `rails new -h` outputs the help for the new command.

Inside a Rails application it works mostly as before. The only change is that calling plain `bin/rails` now only outputs the common commands and not the extended commands.

- `bin/rails`    outputs the help for the common commands
- `bin/rails -h` outputs the help for the common commands and the
  extended commands

### Additional information

This was previously submitted in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/41425 but that PR was stale and I can no longer access the branch.

Fixes: #40823

### Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

* [x] This Pull Request is related to one change. Changes that are unrelated should be opened in separate PRs.
* [x] There are no typos in commit messages and comments.
* [x] Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: `[Fix #issue-number]`
* [x] Feature branch is up-to-date with `main` (if not - rebase it).
* [x] Pull request only contains one commit for bug fixes and small features. If it's a larger feature, multiple commits are permitted but must be descriptive.
* [x] Tests are added if you fix a bug or add a feature.
* [x] CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.
* [x] PR is not in a draft state.
* [x] CI is passing.

pr_comments:
Hey @jonathanhefner, you did the original review of #41425.
Do you think this is good to go?
Or are there things that can be approved?
If you have the time to do a review 😄

Thanks @jonathanhefner for the extensive review 🙇 
I'll make the suggested changes.

> Currently (in this PR), `rails help` and `bin/rails help` output the common commands only. I think it would be good to make them output the extended commands too, the same as `rails -h`.

I tried implementing this for calling `rails help` outside a rails application directory.
But even showing the extended commands requires an application directory to load the Rake tasks.
Without these the rails command fails.
Maybe I can get it to work by requiring the tasks.

> One more thing that I wanted to point out: if a user types rails my_cool_app (instead of rails new my_cool_app) outside of a Rails app directory, they will still be shown the help for rails new. I think that is very good. It might be worth adding a test for it.

If I run `rails generate -h` outside a Rails app directory I also get the help for rails new.
Which is kind of confusing when the USAGE states:
`All commands can be run with -h (or --help) for more information.`

> But even showing the extended commands requires an application directory to load the Rake tasks.
> Without these the rails command fails.
> Maybe I can get it to work by requiring the tasks.

I suppose that instead of trying to unify the behavior regardless of working directory, we could embrace the dichotomy.  For example, outside of an app directory, all help commands (`rails`, `rails -h`, `rails help`) could print:

```
You must specify a command:

  new          Create a new Rails application. "rails new my_app" creates a
               new application called MyApp in "./my_app"
  plugin new   Create a new Rails railtie or engine

Inside a Rails application directory, some common commands are:

  console      Start the Rails console
  server       Start the Rails server
  test         Run tests except system tests

All commands can be run with -h (or --help) for more information.
```

And, inside an app directory, all help commands could print:

```
You must specify a command. The most common commands are:

  generate     Generate new code (short-cut alias: "g")
  console      Start the Rails console (short-cut alias: "c")
  server       Start the Rails server (short-cut alias: "s")
  test         Run tests except system tests (short-cut alias: "t")
  test:system  Run system tests
  dbconsole    Start a console for the database specified in config/database.yml
               (short-cut alias: "db")
  plugin new   Create a new Rails railtie or engine

All commands can be run with -h (or --help) for more information.

In addition to those commands, there are:

#{extended_command_list}
```

(Kind of related to your changes in #46837.)

> > One more thing that I wanted to point out: if a user types rails my_cool_app (instead of rails new my_cool_app) outside of a Rails app directory, they will still be shown the help for rails new. I think that is very good. It might be worth adding a test for it.
>
> If I run `rails generate -h` outside a Rails app directory I also get the help for rails new.
> Which is kind of confusing when the USAGE states:
> `All commands can be run with -h (or --help) for more information.`

I think splitting the commands like above or in #46837 helps with that.

Also, revisiting what I said about `rails my_cool_app`, it might be nice to prepend a "Did you mean?" to the `rails new` help.  For example:

```console
$ rails my_cool_app
Did you mean `rails new my_cool_app`?

Usage:
  rails new APP_PATH [options]

Options:
...
```

That might offer a clue if a user runs `rails generate -h` outside of an app directory, because it would print "Did you mean \`rails new generate\`?".

But I think that can be investigated in a separate PR.

@jonathanhefner I've split the commands to inside and outside the application.
Adding DidYouMean to `rails my_cool_app` is something I could pick after this.

issue_context.title: No way to list common rails commands from CLI outside a rails app directory
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce - `rails --help` - `rails help` - `rails -h` ### Expected behavior Using `rails --help` should print usage instructions for common Rails commands. ``` rails --help ```
Command output 
The most common rails commands are:
 generate     Generate new code (short-cut alias: "g")
 console      Start the Rails console (short-cut alias: "c")
 server       Start the Rails server (short-cut alias: "s")
 test         Run tests except system tests (short-cut alias: "t")
 test:system  Run system tests
 dbconsole    Start a console for the database specified in config/database.yml
              (short-cut alias: "db")

All commands can be run with -h (or --help) for more information.
In addition to those commands, there are:
### Actual behavior It prints usage instructions specific to `rails new` instead. ``` rails --help ```
Command output 
Usage:
  rails new APP_PATH [options]

Options:
      [--skip-namespace], [--no-skip-namespace]              # Skip namespace (affects only isolated engines)
      [--skip-collision-check], [--no-skip-collision-check]  # Skip collision check
  -r, [--ruby=PATH]                                          # Path to the Ruby binary of your choice
                                                             # Default: /Users/olivierlacan/.rbenv/versions/2.7.2/bin/ruby
  -m, [--template=TEMPLATE]                                  # Path to some application template (can be a filesystem path or URL)
  -d, [--database=DATABASE]                                  # Preconfigure for selected database (options: mysql/postgresql/sqlite3/oracle/sqlserver/jdbcmysql/jdbcsqlite3/jdbcpostgresql/jdbc)
                                                             # Default: sqlite3
      [--skip-gemfile], [--no-skip-gemfile]                  # Don't create a Gemfile
  -G, [--skip-git], [--no-skip-git]                          # Skip .gitignore file
      [--skip-keeps], [--no-skip-keeps]                      # Skip source control .keep files
  -M, [--skip-action-mailer], [--no-skip-action-mailer]      # Skip Action Mailer files
      [--skip-action-mailbox], [--no-skip-action-mailbox]    # Skip Action Mailbox gem
      [--skip-action-text], [--no-skip-action-text]          # Skip Action Text gem
  -O, [--skip-active-record], [--no-skip-active-record]      # Skip Active Record files
      [--skip-active-job], [--no-skip-active-job]            # Skip Active Job
      [--skip-active-storage], [--no-skip-active-storage]    # Skip Active Storage files
  -P, [--skip-puma], [--no-skip-puma]                        # Skip Puma related files
  -C, [--skip-action-cable], [--no-skip-action-cable]        # Skip Action Cable files
  -S, [--skip-sprockets], [--no-skip-sprockets]              # Skip Sprockets files
      [--skip-spring], [--no-skip-spring]                    # Don't install Spring application preloader
      [--skip-listen], [--no-skip-listen]                    # Don't generate configuration that depends on the listen gem
  -J, [--skip-javascript], [--no-skip-javascript]            # Skip JavaScript files
      [--skip-turbolinks], [--no-skip-turbolinks]            # Skip turbolinks gem
      [--skip-jbuilder], [--no-skip-jbuilder]                # Skip jbuilder gem
  -T, [--skip-test], [--no-skip-test]                        # Skip test files
      [--skip-system-test], [--no-skip-system-test]          # Skip system test files
      [--skip-bootsnap], [--no-skip-bootsnap]                # Skip bootsnap gem
      [--dev], [--no-dev]                                    # Set up the application with Gemfile pointing to your Rails checkout
      [--edge], [--no-edge]                                  # Set up the application with Gemfile pointing to Rails repository
      [--master], [--no-master]                              # Set up the application with Gemfile pointing to Rails repository master branch
      [--rc=RC]                                              # Path to file containing extra configuration options for rails command
      [--no-rc], [--no-no-rc]                                # Skip loading of extra configuration options from .railsrc file
      [--api], [--no-api]                                    # Preconfigure smaller stack for API only apps
      [--minimal], [--no-minimal]                            # Preconfigure a minimal rails app
  -B, [--skip-bundle], [--no-skip-bundle]                    # Don't run bundle install
  --webpacker, [--webpack=WEBPACK]                           # Preconfigure Webpack with a particular framework (options: react, vue, angular, elm, stimulus)
      [--skip-webpack-install], [--no-skip-webpack-install]  # Don't run Webpack install

Runtime options:
  -f, [--force]                    # Overwrite files that already exist
  -p, [--pretend], [--no-pretend]  # Run but do not make any changes
  -q, [--quiet], [--no-quiet]      # Suppress status output

Rails options:
  -h, [--help], [--no-help]        # Show this help message and quit
  -v, [--version], [--no-version]  # Show Rails version number and quit

Description:
    The 'rails new' command creates a new Rails application with a default
    directory structure and configuration at the path you specify.

    You can specify extra command-line arguments to be used every time
    'rails new' runs in the .railsrc configuration file in your home directory,
    or in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rails/railsrc if XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set.

    Note that the arguments specified in the .railsrc file don't affect the
    defaults values shown above in this help message.

Example:
    rails new ~/Code/Ruby/weblog

    This generates a skeletal Rails installation in ~/Code/Ruby/weblog.
### System configuration **Rails version**: 6.1.0 **Ruby version**: 2.7.2 It seems like there's a bad assumption in `Rails::Command#invoke` where we think the `command_name` could be `--help` but it can't be at the root (`rails --help` without a subcommand) since this conditional will always assign `command_name` to `"application"`: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/95a8c83d2ec7aa34ab127f7fa6def4d8891eb662/railties/lib/rails/command.rb#L31-L41 Since the `command_name` is set (incorrectly IMO) to `"application"`, a call to `rails --help` results in the instantiation of a `Rails::Command::ApplicationCommand` https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/95a8c83d2ec7aa34ab127f7fa6def4d8891eb662/railties/lib/rails/command.rb#L48-L51 When `#perform` is called on that instance, the `help` method "punts" to `Rails::Generators::AppGenerator` with no arguments, which is why we end up with `rails new` usage instructions, which are somewhat helpful, although quite verbose and unrelated to our request (IMO, again). Try as I might I couldn't find how to print the `USAGE` from `HelpCommand` [which clearly exists](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/95a8c83d2ec7aa34ab127f7fa6def4d8891eb662/railties/lib/rails/commands/help/USAGE#L1-L16) and which I definitely remember seeing in the past. Not with `rails` and no arguments (prints `rails new` usage), not with `rails help` no with `rails commands`. This is problematic because it means for someone new to the Rails command line, there's no way to list available commands. The only solution is to look up [the Rails Guide](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/command_line.html#command-line-basics) or trudge through the source (which seems unlikely for newcomers).
comments:
Yes, let's fix this!

To be clear, is this from within an app directory or outside like the home directory?
This example was from the rails command as a standalone RubyGem in my user home directory, not within a created Rails app root directory.

One argument to your proposal could be that none of the commands actually work, or are relevant outside of a Rails application. I'm not sure it's useful showing a new user a long list of commands that don't do anything, or that would result in errors if run. The only one that does work outside a Rails app is the `new` command, which is why you get this help. Once inside a Rails application, the `rails --help` will display the full list of commands.

**tldr;** I think it's working as intended.

I can see it can be confusing to have the same command behave differently. 
Maybe we should have a ‘rails-new’ command instead?

I’ve also had this happen inside an app directory when I deleted the bin directory, trying to debug binstubs. Without bin/rails, Rails no longer thinks you are in an app directory and only allows ‘rails new’.

It would have been nice to have a ‘rails doctor’ command. Similar to ‘brew doctor’.

@aar0nr I take your point but regardless of usability, it should be possible to ask Rails to list its available commands rather than ignore input.

If the `rails` command is ignoring `--help` for any reason it should say so explicitely: 

Example:
```
cd ~
rails --help
$ rails --help
Only the `rails new` command works outside of a rails application directory.

You can use `rails new --help` for help on how to create new Rails application.

The most common rails commands are:
 generate     Generate new code (short-cut alias: "g")
 console      Start the Rails console (short-cut alias: "c")
 server       Start the Rails server (short-cut alias: "s")
 test         Run tests except system tests (short-cut alias: "t")
 test:system  Run system tests
 dbconsole    Start a console for the database specified in config/database.yml
              (short-cut alias: "db")

 new          Create a new Rails application. "rails new my_app" creates a
              new application called MyApp in "./my_app"

# ...
```

This is also a neat possible future tie in for any `rails new --interactive` options as mentioned in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/39444 and https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/interactive-rails-new/74355/22.

Essentially what I'm describing here is what could be in a `rails` manpage: 

```
$ man rails
No manual entry for rails
```

I don't think we want a new command but I agree with @olivierlacan that we should explicitly tell people that if they are not seeing the full list of commands is because they are either outside a Rails app or without the binstub.
@p8 do you want to work on that?
@p8 Down to pair on it if you’d like too by the way. Been diving in that code a bit.
@olivierlacan I'm currently off for the holidays, but I'll have time to work on this in january.
